book_title: All the Men I Never Married
subject_line: The numbered poems of All the Men I Never Married
email_body:
Dear Kim,

I've been reading about All the Men I Never Married, the collection that won the 2022 Forward Prize for Best Collection, and was struck by its form: 48 numbered poems working through everyday sexism and past relationships.

I'd love to ask how the numbering came about, and whether it gave you a kind of distance or a kind of pressure while writing such personal material.

subject_line: Stanage Edge and the title of Black Car Burning
email_body:
Dear Helen,

I learned that Black Car Burning takes its title from a notoriously hard climb at Stanage Edge, and that Caron's fixation on that route sits alongside a strand reaching back to April 1989 and Hillsborough.

I'd be curious to hear how a climbing route became the frame for a Sheffield novel about trust and inherited trauma, and how that thread carried on into A Line Above the Sky.

subject_line: The notebook pages in Ghost Town
email_body:
Dear Jeff,

Ghost Town takes readers through the Liverpool of your childhood, through arcades, vanished tenements and oyster bars, and I noticed that the chapters are divided by photographs that, like the memories themselves, don't follow a chronological order.

Coming from more than twenty radio plays, how did you find a shape for memoir, and what led you to share pages from your notebooks in the paperback?

subject_line: Barnsley as a character in Pity
email_body:
Dear Andrew,

I read that in Pity you wanted Barnsley to be more than a setting, and that the novel sets the voices of Alex, Brian and Simon against the field notes of academics who arrive to chart the town's history.

I'd like to ask about that outsider's voice: what did it let you say about who gets to tell a former mining town's story that the family's voices alone could not?

subject_line: From Sunderland's cold to the heat of Milk Teeth
email_body:
Dear Jessica,

After Saltwater, with its cold, industrial places and a young woman from Sunderland finding her way in London, I read that you wanted Milk Teeth to feel humid and sunlit, following its narrator from the north-east to Barcelona.

I'd love to explore that shift in climate: how did writing heat change the way you approached class, the body and shame on the page?

I read that the idea came from the 2017 City of Culture light show on Victoria Square. How did that night turn into a novel, and how did thirty years of teaching in Hull feed into it?

Why tell a cult story through the wives rather than through an outsider, and why a fictional settlement in the Scottish Highlands?

Having been the first writer-in-residence at Abbey House Museum, how much does working with the city's real history shape what happens to your characters?

I'd love to ask how the intimate family story and the vast scientific question shaped each other as you wrote.

subject_line: Piecing together Clio Campbell in Scabby Queen
email_body:
Dear Kirstin,

Scabby Queen opens with Clio Campbell, one-hit wonder and political activist, found dead three days before her fifty-first birthday, and then builds her life back up from the people around her. That choice to approach a protest singer only through others' memories stayed with me.

I'd be interested to ask how you decided which voices got to tell Clio's story, and whose perspective you deliberately left out.

subject_line: Jack Paton's notebook songs in That Beautiful Atlantic Waltz
email_body:
Dear Malachy,

In That Beautiful Atlantic Waltz, Jack Paton has loved country music for decades yet kept his own songs inside a notebook, and I was intrigued that those songs then left the page as a companion album recorded with Shetland musicians. Writing both a character and his songwriting must have been an unusual double task.

I'd like to ask how writing Jack's songs changed the way you understood him on the page.

subject_line: Caleb at the beef plant in Easy Meat
email_body:
Dear Rachel,

Easy Meat places Caleb in a beef processing plant in June 2016, in the crunch time of the Brexit vote, while he tries to get his life back on track. Setting a man's private struggle against that particular month gives the novel a real sense of a tipping point.

I'd love to ask why you chose the meat plant as Caleb's workplace, and what that setting let you say about the moment.

subject_line: The Raj and Wales side by side in Dignity
email_body:
Dear Alys,

Dignity moves between India and Wales to look at the legacy of the Raj, and how imperialism's effects run through both past and present. Setting that history partly in Wales, rather than only in India, gives the novel an unusual angle on whose story empire is.

I'd like to ask how you came to connect the Welsh setting with the Raj, and how teaching creative writing in Bangor feeds your fiction.

book_title: My Body Can House Two Hearts
subject_line: Two hearts, Welsh and Iraqi, in your debut pamphlet
email_body:
Dear Hanan,

My Body Can House Two Hearts explores belonging across your Welsh and Iraqi heritage, and the title itself seems to answer the question of having to choose. Reading it now, alongside your role as National Poet of Wales and the first Muslim to hold it, gives those poems a different resonance.

I'd be interested to ask how the role has changed the way you think about the belonging those early poems explore.

subject_line: Hannah Adger's summer of 1993 in The Raptures
email_body:
Dear Jan,

The Raptures is narrated by Hannah Adger, the anxious eleven-year-old only child of Evangelical Protestants, in a rural Northern Irish community in the summer of 1993. I was interested to read that the Pied Piper story was part of its inspiration.

I'd love to ask how that old tale shaped the novel, and why a child's voice felt right for a place so bound up with belief.

subject_line: Three Belfast mothers in The Benefactors
email_body:
Dear Wendy,

The Benefactors follows three Belfast women whose eighteen-year-old sons are accused of sexual assault, and its polyphonic approach lets wealth and class show through each of their voices. I also read that you still teach English at a Belfast secondary school, which made me wonder about the teenagers at the novel's edges.

I'd like to ask why you kept the mothers, rather than the sons, at the centre.
